clues.text: Research by Basset-Jones and Lloyd says this thinker’s most famous idea is not applicable to the workplace.
This psychologist examined the relationship between mechanistic science and human behavior in his work The Psychology of Science: A Reconnaissance.
Heavily influenced in his theories by the book The Organism, this psychologist who described one aspect of his theory as “instinctoid” characterized his work as the “third force” in psychology.
This thinker identified B-cognition, a type of thinking that connects the individual to what they are perceiving.
This thinker contrasted D-cognition with B-cognition that allows one to understand contradictory impressions, which occurs during peak experiences.

This author of A Theory of Human Motivation claimed that people have “peak experiences” as a period of interconnectedness and joy, and this man studied “exemplary people” such as Albert Einstein and Frederick Douglass.

clues.text: Richard Katz believed that this psychologist failed to cite time studying the Giving Ceremony of the Blackfoot.
This man's ideas influenced George Leonard's Human Potential Movement.
Douglas McGregor expanded on the ideas in this man’s Eupsychian("yoo-SIKE-ee-un") Management to create the Theory X and Theory Y management styles.
This psychologist imagined a culturally healthy utopia called Eupsychia (“yew-sike-ee-uh”) in a “Theory Z” outlining the ideal organization of companies.
This man’s most famous concept was adapted by Clayton Alderfer’s ERG theory.
A cognitive bias of repeatedly using the same tool for different problems is called this psychologist’s “Hammer.”
This man contrasted the difference between D and B-values, stating that the latter drives metamotivation in people.
A group of people studied by this psychologist have Being-values that define their metamotivations and may have “peak experiences.”
In his work “A Theory of Human Motivation,” this man created a model that can be visualized as a pyramid with self-actualization at the top and physiological needs at the bottom.
Name this psychologist who ranked human desires into a "hierarchy of needs."
